turns.content: I want to paint my living room but I've never painted before. How hard is it really?
Very doable as a first project. The outcome is 80% about prep and 20% about the painting itself. Rushing the prep is what makes amateur paint jobs look amateur.
Filling holes and cracks with spackle, sanding smooth, cleaning the walls, and taping off trim, baseboards, and outlets. Also move furniture to the center and lay down drop cloths.
How do I pick the right paint?

Finish first: flat or matte hides imperfections (good for ceilings), eggshell is ideal for living rooms (some sheen, scrubbable), semi-gloss for trim and doors. Then color — get sample pots and test them on the actual wall in different lighting before committing.
How many coats will I need?
Almost always two. One coat rarely gives you even coverage. If you're going from a dark color to a light one, you may need a primer coat first or a paint-and-primer combo.
What tools do I actually need?

Roller (9-inch, 3/8 nap for smooth walls), roller tray, angled brush for cutting in around edges, painter's tape, drop cloths, a paint stick, and a small spackle knife. Don't cheap out on the brush — it makes a huge difference.

Painting the edges where the roller can't reach — corners, along the ceiling line, around trim. You do it with a brush before rolling. The key is a steady hand and keeping paint just off the tape edge.
How long does a room typically take?
For a standard living room, expect half a day for prep and taping, then an hour or two per coat with drying time in between. Budget a full weekend to do it right without rushing.
Any mistakes I should definitely avoid?

Not stirring the paint enough, skipping the second coat, and peeling the tape before the paint is fully dry. For the tape: pull it back at a 45-degree angle slowly while the paint is still slightly tacky for the cleanest line.
